paragraphs.heading: The probe that went to Pluto
paragraphs.text: New Horizons is a NASA space probe sent out under the New Frontiers program. It launched in 2006 and became the first spacecraft to fly past Pluto and its moons and photograph them in high resolution. Engineers at the Southwest Research Institute and at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) designed it. Alan Stern led the team.

paragraphs.heading: A fast start
paragraphs.text: It left Cape Canaveral on January 19, 2006, on an Atlas V rocket, aimed straight onto a path that would carry it away from both Earth and the Sun. Measured by average speed relative to Earth, it was the fastest object people had ever launched from Earth. The Parker Solar Probe, though, holds the record for top spacecraft speed. On February 28, 2007 New Horizons passed Jupiter at a distance of 2.3 million kilometers. Jupiter's gravity sped it up, and the flyby also tested its instruments, returning data on the planet's atmosphere, moons and magnetosphere.

paragraphs.heading: A long sleep
paragraphs.text: For most of the trip after Jupiter the probe hibernated to protect its systems, waking only for short yearly checkouts. On December 6, 2014, the team brought it back online and began checking its instruments. The approach to Pluto started on January 15, 2015.

paragraphs.heading: Pluto at last
paragraphs.text: On July 14, 2015, New Horizons flew 12,500 km above the surface of Pluto. It was the first spacecraft to explore the dwarf planet. The last of the data from the Pluto flyby reached Earth on October 25, 2016.

paragraphs.heading: Into the Kuiper belt
paragraphs.text: After Pluto, the team steered the probe toward Arrokoth, an object in the Kuiper belt then nicknamed Ultima Thule. It flew past on January 1, 2019, about 6.49 billion km from the Sun. It is still crossing the Kuiper belt, and in April 2026 it was about 9.64 billion km from the Sun. NASA plans to keep it running until it leaves the Kuiper belt, which is expected in 2028 or 2029.

paragraphs.heading: The mission that nearly wasn't
paragraphs.text: New Horizons was chosen for funding in November 2001. Then NASA's new administrator, Sean O'Keefe, left it out of the 2003 budget, which in effect canceled it. After a hard campaign for support, the Planetary Science Decadal Survey came out in summer 2002. This ranked wish list from the scientific community put New Horizons at the top of the medium-size missions, ahead of missions to the Moon and to Jupiter. Once the report was out, the money was finally secured.
